content: 1. Bacteremia caused by Enterococcus faecalis: For strains susceptible to ampicillin or penicillin: Preferred regimen: Administer ampicillin 2 g intravenously (IV) every 4–6 hours. Alternative regimen: Administer ampicillin 2 g IV every 4–6 hours in combination with gentamicin 1 mg/kg IV or intramuscularly (IM) every 8 hours. For ampicillin-resistant and vancomycin-susceptible strains, or in cases of penicillin allergy: Preferred regimen: Administer vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV every 12 hours in combination with gentamicin 1 mg/kg IV/IM every 8 hours. Alternative regimens include linezolid 600 mg IV every 12 hours or daptomycin 6 mg/kg IV every 24 hours. For strains resistant to both ampicillin and vancomycin: Preferred regimen: Linezolid 600 mg IV every 12 hours or daptomycin 6 mg/kg IV every 24 hours. 2. Endocarditis caused by Enterococcus faecalis in adults: For strains susceptible to penicillin, gentamicin, and vancomycin: Preferred regimen: Administer ampicillin 12 g IV daily (divided doses) for 4–6 weeks, or aqueous crystalline penicillin G sodium 18–30 million units (MU) IV daily (divided doses) for 4–6 weeks, in combination with gentamicin sulfate 3 mg/kg IV/IM daily for 4–6 weeks. Alternative regimen: Administer vancomycin hydrochloride 30 mg/kg IV daily (divided doses) for 6 weeks in combination with gentamicin sulfate 3 mg/kg IV/IM daily for 6 weeks. Note: For native valve endocarditis with symptoms ≤3 months, a 4-week course of therapy is recommended. For symptoms >3 months or prosthetic valve involvement, a minimum of 6 weeks of therapy is advised. 3. Meningitis caused by Enterococcus faecalis: For ampicillin-susceptible strains: Preferred regimen: Administer ampicillin 12 g/day IV (divided doses every 4 hours) in combination with gentamicin 5 mg/kg/day IV (divided doses every 8 hours). For ampicillin-resistant strains: Preferred regimen: Administer vancomycin 30–45 mg/kg/day IV (divided doses every 8–12 hours) in combination with gentamicin 5 mg/kg/day IV (divided doses every 8 hours). For strains resistant to both ampicillin and vancomycin: Preferred regimen: Administer linezolid 600 mg IV every 12 hours. 4. Urinary tract infections caused by Enterococcus faecalis: Preferred regimens: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg orally (PO) every 6 hours for 5 days. Fosfomycin 3 g PO as a single dose. Amoxicillin 875 mg to 1 g PO every 12 hours for 5 days. 5. Intra-abdominal or wound infections caused by Enterococcus faecalis: Preferred regimens: Penicillin or ampicillin. Alternative regimens for penicillin allergy or high-level penicillin resistance: Vancomycin. For complicated skin-structure or intra-abdominal infections: Tigecycline 100 mg IV as a single dose, followed by 50 mg IV every 12 hours. 6. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infections: For bacteremia or endocarditis in adults: Preferred regimens: Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV every 8–12 hours. Daptomycin 6 mg/kg/dose IV daily. Alternative regimens: Linezolid 600 mg IV/PO every 12 hours. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 6–12 mg TMP/kg/day divided every 12 hours (if susceptible). 7. Pediatric dosing for vancomycin: Neonates (<4 weeks): For postnatal age ≤7 days and <1200 g: Vancomycin 15 mg/kg/day IV every 24 hours. For postnatal age ≤7 days and 1200–2000 g: Vancomycin 10–15 mg/kg IV every 12–18 hours. For postnatal age >7 days and >2000 g: Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV every 8 hours. Infants and children (>4 weeks): Vancomycin 40 mg/kg/day IV divided every 6–8 hours. 8. Cellulitis in adults: Preferred regimens: Clindamycin 300–450 mg PO three times daily (tid). Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 1–2 double-strength (DS) tablets PO twice daily (bid). Doxycycline 100 mg PO bid. Minocycline 200 mg as a single dose, then 100 mg PO bid. Linezolid 600 mg PO bid.
